patient.name: Tomasz Kowalski
patient.complaint: Two days of a painful red right eye, light sensitivity and blurred vision
background: Two years of low back pain and morning stiffness, never investigated
No contact lenses, no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a painful red eye, photophobia, ciliary flush and a small irregular pupil in a young adult with back pain or another HLA-B27 clue; the pupil separates it from angle closure glaucoma.

points: Tomasz, 29, has a **painful red right eye** for 2 days.
Bright light is **agony**; vision is blurred.
No discharge, no grittiness, no trauma.
Two years of **back pain and morning stiffness** that eases with exercise.

steps.lead: Pain plus photophobia in a red eye means the inside of the eye is inflamed: Tomasz most likely has **anterior uveitis (iritis)**.
His inflammatory back pain shouts **ankylosing spondylitis**, the strongest association with anterior uveitis.

points: Redness is a **ring around the cornea** (ciliary flush).
Slit lamp: **cells and flare** in the anterior chamber.

steps.lead: Tomasz has the full anterior picture: pain, photophobia, **ciliary flush**, blurred vision, small irregular pupil and **cells and flare**.

steps.q: Which pupil finding best separates Tomasz's uveitis from acute angle closure glaucoma?
steps.r: Uveitis gives a **small, irregular pupil** (spasm and synechiae). Angle closure gives a **fixed, mid-dilated** pupil.

steps.lead: Tomasz has no floaters, so this is anterior. **Floaters** and slowly worsening vision suggest **posterior** uveitis; bilateral disease with mouth ulcers suggests **Behçet's**.
If Tomasz's inflammation is not treated quickly, his iris can stick to the lens (**posterior synechiae**), and he risks cataract, glaucoma and vision loss.

steps.text: Do not pick **conjunctivitis** for a red eye with photophobia and blurred vision. Conjunctivitis keeps vision normal and has discharge, not ciliary flush.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (slit-lamp examination by ophthalmology showing cells and flare), or the work-up for an underlying cause: HLA-B27, sacroiliac X-ray, ESR/CRP and chest X-ray for sarcoidosis.

steps.r: Uveitis is a **clinical diagnosis** by ophthalmology; slit lamp shows **cells and flare** in the anterior chamber.

steps.lead: On slit lamp, Tomasz's anterior chamber is full of **inflammatory cells** with hazy **aqueous flare**: that is the diagnosis.

visual.title: Anterior chamber cells (SUN grade)
visual.label: Tomasz 3+
visual.caption: Grading the cells sets a baseline to judge response to drops.

steps.lead: Tomasz's back pain suggests a **systemic** cause, so he gets **HLA-B27**, ESR/CRP and imaging; a chest X-ray looks for sarcoidosis.

steps.title: Tomasz's work-up
steps.text: HLA-B27 positive with sacroiliitis: ankylosing spondylitis is the cause. Normal chest X-ray makes sarcoid unlikely.
In uveitis with inflammatory back pain, the answer is **HLA-B27 and a sacroiliac X-ray**. Hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray points to **sarcoidosis** instead.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': urgent same-day ophthalmology, then topical steroid (prednisolone acetate 1%) plus a cycloplegic (cyclopentolate or atropine); systemic steroids for severe or Behçet's disease.

steps.q: Which combination does the ophthalmologist start for Tomasz's anterior uveitis?
steps.r: **Topical steroid** to settle inflammation plus a **cycloplegic** to stop ciliary spasm and prevent synechiae. Pilocarpine constricts the pupil, the wrong way.

steps.lead: Tomasz is treated as an **emergency**: urgent ophthalmology, **prednisolone acetate 1%** drops and **cyclopentolate** to dilate the pupil and ease pain.

visual.title: Tomasz on drops
visual.caption: Cells clear over weeks; steroid drops are then tapered slowly, not stopped suddenly.

steps.lead: If Tomasz's inflammation were **severe** or failed drops, he would need **oral prednisolone**.
Had both eyes been inflamed with mouth and genital ulcers (**Behçet's**), he would need **high-dose systemic steroid** started urgently.
If Tomasz keeps relapsing, the specialist adds **methotrexate or azathioprine** to control the autoimmune disease long term.

steps.title: Uveitis treatment ladder
nodes: Bilateral with systemic disease (Behçet's) → high-dose systemic steroid
steps.caption: Refer the AS to rheumatology too.

steps.lead: Tomasz's plan follows **RCOphth uveitis guidance** and **NICE CKS Uveitis**: same-day referral, specialist treatment and a rheumatology referral for AS.

visual.title: Intraocular pressure on steroid drops
visual.label: Tomasz 18
visual.caption: Pressure is checked at each visit because steroid drops can raise IOP.

steps.text: A GP should not start steroid drops for a red eye before slit lamp: a **herpes simplex** dendritic ulcer can be made much worse.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why HLA-B27 disease causes anterior uveitis, why flare appears (blood-aqueous barrier breakdown), why the pupil is irregular (posterior synechiae) or how cycloplegics work.

steps.lead: Tomasz's **HLA-B27** links his spine and his eye: shared genes drive **T-cell mediated** inflammation of the anterior uvea.
Inflamed iris vessels leak: the **blood-aqueous barrier** breaks down, so protein (flare) and cells fill Tomasz's aqueous.

steps.title: From inflamed iris to glaucoma
nodes: Sticks to anterior lens capsule (posterior synechiae)
steps.caption: Dilating the pupil early prevents this chain.

steps.lead: Tomasz's irregular pupil is early **posterior synechiae**. Chronic inflammation and steroid drops also raise his risk of **cataract and raised IOP**.
**Cyclopentolate** paralyses Tomasz's ciliary muscle and iris sphincter: less spasm pain, and a dilated pupil cannot stick to the lens.

steps.q: What causes the 'flare' seen in Tomasz's anterior chamber?
o: Protein leaking through a broken blood-aqueous barrier
steps.r: Flare is **protein** in the aqueous, seen as a light beam, from breakdown of the **blood-aqueous barrier**.

steps.text: **Cycloplegic** = paralyses the ciliary muscle (relieves pain); **mydriatic** = dilates the pupil (prevents synechiae). Cyclopentolate and atropine do both.

mcq.r: The uvea is the **iris, ciliary body and choroid**.

mcq.q: Which condition is most strongly associated with anterior uveitis?
mcq.r: **Ankylosing spondylitis** (HLA-B27); also reactive arthritis, sarcoid and IBD.

mcq.q: Which pupil is typical of anterior uveitis?
mcq.r: **Small, irregular** pupil from spasm and synechiae.

mcq.q: Floaters and slowly worsening blurred vision suggest which type?
mcq.r: **Posterior uveitis**, with a risk of retinal detachment.

mcq.q: Bilateral uveitis with mouth and genital ulcers suggests?
What does slit lamp show in anterior uveitis?
mcq.r: **Cells and flare** in the anterior chamber.

mcq.q: Which test looks for sarcoidosis in recurrent uveitis?
Which eye drop is the topical steroid used in uveitis?
Which drugs are used long term for recurrent autoimmune uveitis?

o: Lower IOP by constricting the pupil
Paralyse ciliary muscle and iris sphincter
mcq.r: They relieve **ciliary spasm** and reduce **synechiae** risk.

prompts.q: What is uveitis and which conditions is it associated with?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the three parts and look for the systemic clue.

points.p: Inflammation of the iris, ciliary body and choroid

points.why: The strongest association; ask about back pain.
Arthritis, urethritis and eye disease after infection.

prompts.q: Describe the classic presentation of anterior uveitis.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: photophobia plus a small irregular pupil.

points.why: Angle closure gives a fixed, mid-dilated pupil.

points.p: Cells and flare on slit lamp

prompts.q: How do posterior uveitis and Behçet's uveitis present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: floaters mean posterior; bilateral plus systemic means Behçet's.

points.p: Posterior: blurred vision worsening over days
Bilateral uveitis with systemic disease = Behçet's
points.why: Oral and genital ulcers are the clue.

prompts.q: Which features tell you a red eye is anterior uveitis rather than angle closure or conjunctivitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the pupil and the vision decide.

points.p: Small irregular pupil (angle closure: fixed mid-dilated)
Photophobia and blurred vision (conjunctivitis: normal vision)

points.why: Conjunctivitis redness is diffuse with discharge.

prompts.q: What are the complications of uveitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: think what sticks, what clouds and what raises pressure.

points.why: Iris stuck to the lens: irregular pupil.
Secondary angle closure or steroid response.

prompts.q: How is uveitis diagnosed, and what is done if it is recurrent or systemic disease is suspected?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: diagnosis is clinical; tests look for the cause.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis by ophthalmology on slit lamp

prompts.q: What is the first-line management of anterior uveitis?

points.why: Relieves spasm and dilates the pupil.

prompts.q: How do you escalate treatment for severe, Behçet's or recurrent uveitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: topical → oral → high-dose systemic → immunosuppressant.

points.p: Bilateral with severe systemic disease (Behçet's): high-dose systemic steroid urgently

prompts.q: Why does HLA-B27 cause uveitis, and why do you see cells and flare?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: genetics → T cells → leaky barrier.

points.p: Shared genetic predisposition causing T-cell mediated inflammation

points.why: Lets protein and cells into the aqueous.
Flare is the light beam made visible.

prompts.q: How do synechiae and glaucoma develop, and how do cycloplegics help?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a dilated pupil cannot stick to the lens.

points.p: Inflamed iris adheres to the anterior lens capsule
Risk of secondary angle closure glaucoma
Steroids and chronic inflammation: cataract and raised IOP
Cycloplegics paralyse ciliary muscle and iris sphincter

glossary.uvea: The pigmented middle layer of the eye: iris, ciliary body and choroid.
glossary.iritis: Anterior uveitis: inflammation of the iris.
glossary.anterior uveitis: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body; the commonest form of uveitis.
glossary.posterior uveitis: Inflammation of the choroid, often with floaters and retina involvement.
glossary.ciliary body: Ring of muscle behind the iris that focuses the lens and makes aqueous humour.
glossary.choroid: Vascular layer between the retina and sclera.
glossary.ciliary flush: Redness concentrated in a ring around the cornea, typical of intraocular inflammation.
glossary.Photophobia: Pain or discomfort caused by light.
glossary.cells and flare: Slit-lamp signs of inflammatory cells and protein in the anterior chamber.
glossary.anterior chamber: Fluid-filled space between the cornea and the iris.
glossary.aqueous humour: Clear fluid that fills the front of the eye.
glossary.blood-aqueous barrier: Tight junctions in iris and ciliary vessels that keep protein and cells out of the aqueous.
glossary.slit lamp: A microscope with a bright beam used to examine the eye in detail.
glossary.Floaters: Moving specks in the vision caused by cells or debris in the vitreous.
glossary.retinal detachment: Separation of the retina from the back of the eye; sight-threatening.
glossary.posterior synechiae: Adhesions between the iris and the front of the lens, giving an irregular pupil.
glossary.iris bombé: Forward bowing of the iris from trapped aqueous when synechiae seal the pupil.
glossary.glaucoma: Optic nerve damage, usually from raised intraocular pressure.
glossary.IOP: Intraocular pressure; normal is about 10 to 21 mmHg.
glossary.Ankylosing spondylitis: HLA-B27 linked inflammatory arthritis of the spine and sacroiliac joints.
glossary.HLA-B27: A gene variant linked to ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis and anterior uveitis.
glossary.sacroiliitis: Inflammation of the sacroiliac joints, seen on X-ray or MRI in AS.
glossary.Reactive arthritis: Arthritis after a gut or genital infection, with conjunctivitis or uveitis.
glossary.Sarcoidosis: Multisystem non-caseating granulomas; causes uveitis and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
glossary.IBD: Inflammatory bowel disease: Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis.
glossary.Behçet's: Vasculitis with oral and genital ulcers and bilateral uveitis.
glossary.prednisolone acetate: Steroid eye drop used first-line in anterior uveitis.
glossary.Cycloplegic: Drug that paralyses the ciliary muscle, relieving spasm.
glossary.cyclopentolate: Short-acting cycloplegic and mydriatic eye drop.
glossary.atropine: Long-acting cycloplegic and mydriatic eye drop.
glossary.methotrexate: Steroid-sparing immunosuppressant used for recurrent autoimmune uveitis.
glossary.azathioprine: Steroid-sparing immunosuppressant; check TPMT before starting.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate; a non-specific marker of inflammation.
glossary.visual acuity: Sharpness of vision measured on a Snellen chart (e.g. 6/6).
glossary.dendritic ulcer: Branching corneal ulcer of herpes simplex; worsened by steroid drops.

technique.stem: A 27 year old man has a 2 day history of a painful red left eye with marked photophobia and blurred vision. He has had low back pain and stiffness for 18 months that is worst in the morning. There is redness around the cornea and the left pupil is small and irregular. There is no discharge.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a painful red eye: look at the pupil and the systemic clue.
Photophobia + blurred vision = intraocular. Inflammatory back pain = **AS**. Ciliary flush + small irregular pupil = iritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anterior uveitis** linked to ankylosing spondylitis.

elim: Angle closure gives a **fixed, mid-dilated** pupil, haloes and vomiting, usually in older long-sighted people.
Bacterial conjunctivitis has discharge and normal vision.
Episcleritis is mild with no photophobia or pupil change.
HSV keratitis gives a dendritic ulcer and watering; no link to back pain.

steps.x: **B. Anterior uveitis.** Rule: red eye + photophobia + small irregular pupil + back pain = HLA-B27 uveitis.

technique.stem: A 34 year old woman has her third episode of anterior uveitis in 2 years. She has a dry cough, tender red shins and has recently felt breathless on exertion. There is no back pain.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation for the underlying cause?

steps.x: Investigation for the cause of recurrent uveitis: match the systemic clue to the test.
Recurrent uveitis plus cough, erythema nodosum and breathlessness = **sarcoidosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chest X-ray** for bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

elim: CT head does not look for sarcoid or HLA-B27 disease.
HLA-B27 is for AS-type disease; there is no back pain.
Sacroiliac X-ray is for suspected ankylosing spondylitis.
Urine culture is not part of uveitis work-up here.

steps.x: **A. Chest X-ray.** Rule: recurrent uveitis + chest symptoms = CXR for sarcoid.

technique.stem: A 30 year old man is seen in eye casualty with acute anterior uveitis of the right eye. Slit lamp shows cells and flare in the anterior chamber. The cornea stains normally with fluorescein. Intraocular pressure is 16 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Prednisolone acetate 1% and cyclopentolate eye drops

steps.x: Initial management of confirmed anterior uveitis.
Confirmed anterior uveitis. Normal fluorescein excludes a herpes ulcer, so steroids are safe. Pressure is normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Topical steroid plus a cycloplegic**.

elim: Aciclovir is for herpes simplex or zoster eye disease.
Pilocarpine constricts the pupil, increasing synechiae risk; it is for angle closure.
Timolol lowers IOP, which is normal.
Chloramphenicol is for bacterial conjunctivitis.

steps.x: **C. Prednisolone acetate 1% and cyclopentolate.** Rule: uveitis = steroid + cycloplegic.

technique.stem: A 25 year old man with HLA-B27 positive ankylosing spondylitis has anterior uveitis. On slit-lamp examination, the beam of light is visible as it passes through the anterior chamber, like a beam through smoke.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this finding?

steps.x: Mechanism of a slit-lamp sign.
A visible beam in the aqueous is **flare**: protein in the anterior chamber.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Breakdown of the **blood-aqueous barrier** lets protein leak in.

elim: Corneal oedema makes the cornea hazy, not the aqueous beam.
Blood forms a hyphaema level, not flare.
Lens protein leakage is a rare cause, not HLA-B27 uveitis.
Raised IOP does not create flare.

steps.x: **A. Breakdown of the blood-aqueous barrier.** Rule: flare = protein, cells = white cells.

practice.stem: A 32 year old man has a 3 day history of a painful red right eye. Bright lights make the pain worse and his vision is blurred. He has a 2 year history of back pain that improves with exercise. There is circumcorneal redness and the right pupil is small and irregular. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Most likely diagnosis of a painful red eye.

clues: Bright lights make the pain worse
back pain that improves with exercise
steps.x: Photophobia, inflammatory back pain, ciliary flush and a small irregular pupil.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anterior uveitis** (HLA-B27).

elim: Angle closure has a fixed mid-dilated pupil.
Conjunctivitis has normal vision and discharge.
Episcleritis is mild, with normal pupil and vision.
Scleritis pain is worse on eye movement with a violet eye, typically in RA.

steps.x: **B. Anterior uveitis.** Rule: small irregular pupil + photophobia = iritis.

practice.e: Photophobia, ciliary flush and a small irregular pupil with inflammatory back pain is HLA-B27 anterior uveitis. Angle closure would give a fixed mid-dilated pupil.

practice.stem: A 26 year old woman has a painful red left eye with photophobia. Three weeks ago she had diarrhoea after eating at a barbecue. She now has a painful swollen right knee and dysuria.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Anterior uveitis secondary to reactive arthritis

steps.x: Diagnosis that explains the eye and the systemic picture.

clues: diarrhoea after eating at a barbecue
painful swollen right knee and dysuria
steps.x: Post-infective arthritis + urethritis + painful red eye with photophobia = **reactive arthritis** with uveitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anterior uveitis secondary to reactive arthritis**.

elim: Bacterial conjunctivitis lacks photophobia and the systemic picture.
Episcleritis is mild without photophobia; there is no Crohn's history.
Gonococcal conjunctivitis gives profuse purulent discharge.
Scleritis is linked to RA; this is post-infective.

steps.x: **A. Anterior uveitis secondary to reactive arthritis.** Rule: reactive arthritis is a classic uveitis association.

practice.e: Arthritis and urethritis after gastroenteritis is reactive arthritis, an HLA-B27 condition associated with anterior uveitis.

practice.stem: A 41 year old man has a 10 day history of gradually worsening blurred vision in both eyes and many black spots that move across his vision. His eyes are not red or painful. He has recurrent mouth and genital ulcers. His temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Bilateral posterior uveitis due to Behçet's disease

steps.x: Diagnosis of a quiet eye with floaters and falling vision.

clues: gradually worsening blurred vision in both eyes
black spots that move across his vision
steps.x: Floaters and gradual blur = **posterior** uveitis. Bilateral with oral and genital ulcers = **Behçet's**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bilateral posterior uveitis due to Behçet's disease**.

elim: Angle closure is acute, painful and red.
Anterior uveitis is painful and red with photophobia.
CRVO is sudden, usually unilateral, in older hypertensive patients.
Vitreous haemorrhage is sudden, usually diabetic, and not linked to ulcers.

steps.x: **C. Posterior uveitis due to Behçet's.** Rule: floaters = posterior; bilateral + ulcers = Behçet's.

practice.e: Gradual blur and floaters indicate posterior uveitis; bilateral disease with oral and genital ulcers is Behçet's.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman with Crohn's disease has a painful, red right eye with photophobia for 2 days. Visual acuity is 6/12. An ophthalmologist examines her with a slit lamp.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on slit-lamp examination?
o: Cells and flare in the anterior chamber
Shallow anterior chamber with corneal oedema

steps.x: Most likely slit-lamp finding.
IBD + painful red eye with photophobia and reduced vision = **anterior uveitis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cells and flare** in the anterior chamber.

elim: A dendritic ulcer is HSV keratitis.
Drusen are age-related macular degeneration.
Papillae are allergic or bacterial conjunctivitis.
Shallow chamber with corneal oedema is angle closure glaucoma.

steps.x: **A. Cells and flare.** Rule: the defining slit-lamp sign of anterior uveitis.

practice.e: IBD is associated with anterior uveitis, whose defining slit-lamp finding is inflammatory cells and aqueous flare.

practice.stem: A 38 year old man with ankylosing spondylitis has had several episodes of anterior uveitis. On examination the left pupil is irregular and does not dilate evenly with cyclopentolate. His intraocular pressure has risen to 34 mmHg. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of the irregular pupil?

steps.x: Most likely cause of a complication of uveitis.

clues: irregular and does not dilate evenly
steps.x: Recurrent uveitis + irregular pupil that dilates unevenly + raised IOP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Posterior synechiae** (iris stuck to lens), causing secondary angle closure.

elim: Horner's gives a small regular pupil with ptosis.
Optic neuritis gives a RAPD and painful eye movements, not an irregular pupil.
Retinal detachment does not distort the pupil.
Third nerve palsy gives a large round pupil with ptosis and a down-and-out eye.

steps.x: **C. Posterior synechiae.** Rule: irregular pupil after uveitis = synechiae; can cause glaucoma.

practice.e: Recurrent uveitis causes the iris to adhere to the lens (posterior synechiae), giving an irregular pupil and risking secondary angle closure glaucoma.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has a painful red eye with photophobia. He is HLA-B27 positive. His GP is unsure which systemic condition is most likely to be associated.
practice.q: Which systemic condition is most strongly associated with his eye condition?

steps.x: Most likely association of HLA-B27 anterior uveitis.
Painful red eye with photophobia = anterior uveitis; HLA-B27 points to spondyloarthritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ankylosing spondylitis**.

elim: Graves' causes thyroid eye disease: proptosis and lid lag.
Psoriatic arthritis is linked, but skin psoriasis alone is weaker.
RA is linked to scleritis and dry eye, not HLA-B27 uveitis.
Diabetes causes retinopathy.

steps.x: **A. Ankylosing spondylitis.** Rule: uveitis + HLA-B27 = AS until proven otherwise.

practice.e: Anterior uveitis is most strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis (HLA-B27). RA is classically associated with scleritis.

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 1 day history of a painful red right eye with photophobia and blurred vision. Her GP suspects anterior uveitis. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation for suspected uveitis.

clues: painful red right eye with photophobia and blurred vision
steps.x: First episode, classic features. Diagnosis is **clinical by ophthalmology**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Slit-lamp examination** showing cells and flare.

elim: A swab is for infective conjunctivitis.
CT orbits is for orbital cellulitis or trauma.
Fluorescein angiography images retinal vessels, e.g. in diabetic eye disease.
HLA-B27 looks for a cause in recurrent disease; it does not diagnose uveitis.

steps.x: **E. Slit-lamp examination by ophthalmology.** Rule: uveitis is diagnosed on slit lamp.

practice.e: Uveitis is a clinical diagnosis by ophthalmology; slit lamp shows cells and flare. HLA-B27 is for recurrent disease or suspected systemic cause.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man has his second episode of anterior uveitis. He describes 2 years of lower back pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning and better with exercise. Chest examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the underlying cause?
o: HLA-B27 testing and sacroiliac joint X-ray

steps.x: Investigation for the cause of recurrent uveitis.

clues: worse in the morning and better with exercise
steps.x: Recurrent uveitis + inflammatory back pain = suspected **ankylosing spondylitis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **HLA-B27 and a sacroiliac X-ray**.

elim: Anti-CCP is for rheumatoid arthritis.
Chest X-ray looks for sarcoidosis; there are no chest features.
Serum ACE is a sarcoid marker.
Urine dipstick is not useful here.

steps.x: **C. HLA-B27 and sacroiliac X-ray.** Rule: uveitis + inflammatory back pain = test for AS.

practice.e: Recurrent uveitis with inflammatory back pain should prompt HLA-B27 testing and a sacroiliac X-ray for ankylosing spondylitis.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman goes to her GP with a 1 day history of a painful red left eye, photophobia and reduced vision. There is ciliary flush and a small pupil. She has no discharge. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Prednisolone eye drops started by the GP

steps.x: Initial management of suspected uveitis in primary care.

clues: ciliary flush and a small pupil
steps.x: Classic anterior uveitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent same-day ophthalmology referral**: it is an emergency.

elim: Chloramphenicol treats bacterial conjunctivitis.
GPs should not start steroid drops without slit lamp (risk with herpes keratitis).
Delay risks synechiae and vision loss.
Routine referral is too slow.

steps.x: **E. Urgent same-day ophthalmology referral.** Rule: suspected uveitis = eye casualty today.

practice.e: Uveitis is treated as an ophthalmological emergency with urgent referral. Steroid drops should be started by ophthalmology after slit lamp.

practice.stem: A 33 year old man has confirmed acute anterior uveitis of the right eye on slit-lamp examination. There is no corneal ulcer. Intraocular pressure is 15 mmHg. He is in severe pain from ciliary spasm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Prednisolone acetate 1% and cyclopentolate eye drops

steps.x: Initial treatment of confirmed anterior uveitis.
Confirmed, no ulcer, normal pressure, spasm pain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Topical steroid plus cycloplegic** (cyclopentolate).

elim: Aciclovir is for herpetic eye disease.
Oral steroid is second line for severe disease.
Pilocarpine constricts the pupil and worsens synechiae.
Timolol is for raised IOP.

steps.x: **D. Prednisolone acetate 1% and cyclopentolate.** Rule: steroid + cycloplegic.

practice.e: First-line treatment is a topical corticosteroid (prednisolone acetate 1%) plus a cycloplegic such as cyclopentolate to relieve spasm and prevent synechiae.

practice.stem: A 39 year old man with Behçet's disease has bilateral uveitis with falling vision in both eyes, oral ulcers and new skin lesions. Visual acuity is 6/36 in both eyes. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 134/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of the uveitis emergency.
Bilateral, sight-threatening uveitis with severe systemic disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **High-dose systemic corticosteroid** started urgently.

elim: Azathioprine is long-term steroid-sparing therapy; too slow alone.
NSAIDs are for scleritis, not this emergency.
Cycloplegic alone does not control inflammation.
Topical steroid alone is not enough for bilateral posterior disease with systemic involvement.

steps.x: **B. High-dose systemic corticosteroid.** Rule: bilateral uveitis + severe systemic disease = urgent high-dose steroid.

practice.e: Bilateral uveitis with severe systemic disease such as Behçet's needs high-dose systemic corticosteroid started urgently; immunosuppressants follow long term.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman is treated for anterior uveitis with steroid drops and cyclopentolate drops. She asks why she needs the second drop, which makes her vision blurry.
practice.q: Which is the mechanism of benefit of cyclopentolate in uveitis?
o: Constricts the pupil to open the drainage angle
Kills bacteria in the anterior chamber
Paralyses the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter

steps.x: Mechanism of a drug used in uveitis.
Blurred near vision is from loss of accommodation: a **cycloplegic**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: It **paralyses the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter**: relieves spasm and dilates the pupil, preventing synechiae.

elim: That is pilocarpine, the opposite effect.
It is not an antibiotic.
That is timolol.
Steroids reduce leakage; cyclopentolate does not repair the barrier.

steps.x: **C. Paralyses ciliary muscle and iris sphincter.** Rule: cycloplegic = less spasm pain, fewer synechiae.

practice.e: Cyclopentolate is a cycloplegic/mydriatic: it paralyses the ciliary muscle and iris sphincter, relieving spasm and reducing synechiae.
